71.title: Rabia's torch and bucket
71.hook: Rabia of Basra carries fire to burn paradise and water to drown hell, so God is loved for God alone (Attar, Memorial of the Saints)
71.howItsDone: Sufis honor Rabia al-Adawiyya as an early teacher of love for God for God's own sake, and her story and sayings are told in Sufi gatherings and books of saints across the Muslim world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ant and the grasshopper, and the ending people still argue over. Your line was store, and share. Did you put one thing by, and give one thing away? Day seventy-one.

A new week, and a new set of homes: Sufi teachers, desert monks, and the Buddha. We start in the city of Basra, in what's now Iraq, more than twelve hundred years ago. Picture a woman hurrying through the street. In one hand she carries a burning torch. In the other, a bucket of water, sloshing as she goes. People stop and stare. Someone finally asks her the obvious question: where are you going with those? Her answer has been repeated for centuries, by people of many faiths. Today's story is Rabia's torch and bucket.
screen: `BASRA, TWELVE CENTURIES AGO.` → `A TORCH IN ONE HAND.` → `WATER IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Rabia al-Adawiyya lived in Basra in the seven hundreds. She's one of the earliest and best-loved Sufis, the teachers of the inner, mystical path within Islam. Most of what we know about her comes from writers who lived long after her, especially the Persian poet Attar, in his Memorial of the Saints, written around four centuries later. So these are stories told about her, and honest scholars treat them that way. Tradition says she was born poor, was sold into slavery as a girl, and was set free after her master saw her praying through the night. Then comes the torch and the bucket. When they ask her what they're for, she says, as the story is told: I'm going to set fire to paradise, and pour water on the fires of hell, so that both are gone. Then people will worship God not out of fear of punishment, and not out of hope for a reward, but for God alone. It's a startling picture, and it's meant to be. Rabia isn't mocking heaven or hell; she's asking what's underneath our reasons. If the reward vanished, and the threat vanished, would the love still be there? Another saying people attribute to her makes the same point: she wanted to love God for God's own beauty, not as a bargain. You don't have to share her faith to feel the edge of that question in your own life. Most of what we do comes with a receipt attached: the praise, the payback, the good review. But you know the other kind too. A parent rocking a baby at three in the morning. Someone singing alone in the car. Nobody's keeping score. That's the kind of love Rabia was walking through Basra for.
screen: `RABIA OF BASRA, AN EARLY SUFI.` · `BURN PARADISE, DROWN HELL.` · `NO FEAR, NO REWARD — GOD ALONE.` · `LOVE WITHOUT A RECEIPT.` · then, large: `FOR ITS OWN SAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good thing with no reward in mind. Settle, and breathe. First, think of something good you did recently, and notice honestly what you hoped to get back: thanks, a good impression, a favor later. No blame; everyone does it. Now think of one small good thing you could do today that nobody will ever know about. Picture doing it. Picture no one noticing. See how that feels. If you pray, you might simply sit with Rabia's question in silence. The bell holds the time.
Rabia's torch and bucket. Fire for paradise, water for hell, so that what's left is love for its own sake. Today's word.
Your line: for its own sake. Today, do one kind thing and tell nobody. Not later, not ever. Let it be the whole reward. Day seventy-one.

72.title: The elephant in the dark
72.hook: people touch an elephant in a dark room and call it a fan, a pillar, a throne (Rumi, Masnavi 3.1259ff)
72.tomorrow: Abba Moses and the leaking basket
72.howItsDone: Readers of Rumi's Masnavi often tell the elephant in the dark when talking about the limits of what any one person perceives, and teachers in many settings use it to open conversations across disagreement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabia's torch and bucket: fire for paradise, water for hell, and love for God alone. Your line was for its own sake. Did one kind thing go unannounced? Day seventy-two.

Think of a family argument about something that happened years ago. Your sister remembers one thing. Your dad remembers another. You remember a third, and you'd swear to it. Everyone was there. Everyone is sure. And somehow nobody's lying. Each of you touched a different part of the same afternoon. The Persian poet Rumi, writing in the twelve hundreds, told a story about exactly this, set in a dark room, with a very large visitor inside. Today's story is the elephant in the dark.
screen: `EVERYONE WAS THERE.` → `EVERYONE IS SURE.` → `A DARK ROOM, A LARGE VISITOR.`

segments.voice: Rumi tells it in his long poem, the Masnavi, in its third book. Some travelers bring an elephant to a town where no one has ever seen one, and they keep it in a dark house. People crowd in to see it. But it's too dark to see anything, so each one reaches out and touches. One hand finds the trunk: this creature, he says, is like a water pipe. Another finds the ear: no, it's like a fan. Another wraps her arms around a leg: it's a pillar. Another pats the back: it's shaped like a throne. Each description is honest. Each is about something real. And each is wrong about the whole. Then Rumi gives the line the story turns on. If each of them had held a candle, he says, the difference would have gone out of their words. Nobody needed to shout louder. They needed light. Rumi was a Muslim scholar and Sufi teacher, and in the poem he uses the story to say something about the limits of our senses: the hand can only know what it touches. Readers have taken it in many directions since, and people disagree about how far to push it. An older cousin of the story appears in the Buddhist Udana, where a king has blind men describe an elephant, and they end up in a fistfight. So the picture has traveled. Here's where it lands on an ordinary day. When someone describes something completely differently from you, it's possible one of you is simply wrong. But it's also possible you've got the ear, and they've got the leg. Before arguing, bring a candle: ask what their hand is touching.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.` · `A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.` · `WITH A CANDLE, NO DIFFERENCE.` · `ASK WHAT THEIR HAND IS TOUCHING.` · then, large: `BRING A CANDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask one person how they see something. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person who sees some matter differently from you. Not the biggest fight you have; something small and real. Picture the two of you in the dark room, each with a hand on the elephant. Ask yourself, gently: what part might they be touching that I'm not? Then think of one honest question you could ask them today, a question that begins with how do you see it. Just picture asking. The bell holds the time.
The elephant in the dark. Rumi's story of hands in a dark room, each honest, each partial, and the candle that would have ended the argument. Today's word.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT IN THE DARK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bring a candle. Today, when someone sees it differently, ask one question before you argue: what are you touching that I'm not? Day seventy-two.

73.title: Abba Moses and the leaking basket
73.word: Abba Moses and the leaking baske
73.hook: asked to judge a brother, he arrives carrying a basket leaking sand: my own faults run out behind me (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)
73.howItsDone: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers are read in Orthodox, Coptic, Catholic and many Protestant communities, and Abba Moses is honored as a saint; the leaking basket is one of the stories most often told about not judging.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elephant in the dark: a pipe, a fan, a pillar, a throne, and Rumi's candle. Your line was bring a candle. Did you ask someone how they see it? Day seventy-three.

You know the group chat that lights up when someone messes up. Did you hear what he did? Can you believe she said that? Everybody has an opinion, and it's a strange kind of fun, deciding together how wrong someone else was. Now picture the same scene sixteen hundred years ago, in the Egyptian desert. A community of monks has gathered to sit in judgment on one of their brothers. They're only waiting for one more elder to arrive, a big, famous old man named Moses. And when he finally walks in, he's carrying something odd. Today's story is Abba Moses and the leaking basket.
screen: `DID YOU HEAR WHAT HE DID?` → `THE MONKS GATHER TO JUDGE.` → `ONE ELDER IS LATE.`

segments.voice: In the three hundreds, thousands of Christians went out into the deserts of Egypt to live simply and pray. The younger monks called their elders abba, father, and wrote down their short, sharp sayings. Those collections are called the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, and they're still read in monasteries today. Abba Moses is one of the most surprising people in them. Tradition says he came from Ethiopia, was once a servant, and then the leader of a gang of robbers, before he turned up at a monastery and slowly became one of its gentlest elders. Here's the story. A brother at the settlement of Scetis does something wrong. The monks call a council and send for Moses. He doesn't want to come. They send again: everyone is waiting for you. So he gets up and goes. And as he walks in, he's carrying a container full of holes, and something is running out of it behind him the whole way. In the best-known version, it's an old jug, leaking water. In other tellings, it's a basket, trickling sand. The monks come out to meet him and ask: father, what is this? And Moses says, more or less: my own faults are running out behind me, and I don't even see them, and today I've come to judge somebody else's. That's all. And the story says the monks said nothing more to the brother, and forgave him. Notice he doesn't say the brother did nothing wrong. He doesn't give a speech about mercy. He just walks in carrying the truth about himself, where everyone can see it. And the room changes. The trail behind him is the whole sermon.
screen: `THE DESERT FATHERS OF EGYPT.` · `MOSES, ONCE A ROBBER.` · `A CONTAINER FULL OF HOLES.` · `MY FAULTS RUN OUT BEHIND ME.` · then, large: `MY OWN BASKET LEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: skip one judgment today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've been quietly judging. Maybe a coworker, maybe a relative, maybe a stranger online. Don't argue with the judgment; just notice it. Now picture yourself walking toward them carrying Moses's basket, with a thin line of sand running out behind you: a few of your own old mistakes, the ones you'd rather nobody mentioned. Keep walking, and feel what happens to the judgment. You don't have to drop it. Just carry the basket alongside it. The bell holds the time.
Abba Moses and the leaking basket. The desert elder who came to a trial carrying his own faults behind him, and the trial ended. Today's word.
screen: `ABBA MOSES AND THE LEAKING BASKET — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: my own basket leaks. Today, the next time you're about to judge someone out loud, remember the sand running out behind you, and say nothing instead. Day seventy-three.

74.title: Become all flame
74.hook: Abba Lot asks what more he can do, and Abba Joseph raises fingers like lamps: why not become all flame? (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)
74.howItsDone: Monks and many Christians, especially in the Orthodox tradition, read Abba Joseph's saying as a call to be transformed by God completely; lighting a candle before prayer is a common practice in Orthodox and Catholic churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba Moses walked into a trial with sand running out behind him. Your line was my own basket leaks. Did you skip a judgment? Day seventy-four.

Maybe you know this feeling. You've built the good habits. The streak is going. You drink the water, you take the walk, you sit with the bell most days. You're doing the list. And one evening a small question slips in: is this it? Is there something more, and what is it? It's not a complaint. It's a real question, and people have been asking it for a very long time. Sixteen centuries ago, in the Egyptian desert, a monk named Lot asked it out loud, to an older monk named Joseph. And Joseph answered without a single instruction. Today's story is become all flame.
screen: `THE HABITS ARE GOING.` → `IS THIS IT?` → `LOT ASKS JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: It's another story from the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, the same collection as yesterday's leaking basket. Abba Lot comes to visit Abba Joseph, and he lays out his life honestly. As far as I can, he says, I keep my little rule of prayer. I fast a little. I pray, and I keep quiet. As far as I can, I keep my thoughts clean. What else should I do? It's a humble list. Notice the phrase he keeps using: as far as I can. And Joseph doesn't criticize any of it. He stands up. He stretches his hands toward heaven. And the story says his fingers became like ten lamps of fire. And he says to Lot: if you want, you can become all flame. That's the end of the saying. The collection doesn't tell us what Lot did next; the story stops right there, with the fire. For the desert monks, the answer to what more should I do was not another item on the list. The list is good. The list is the fuel. But the point was never to finish the list. It was to be changed by what the list was for, all the way through. Christians read this as the life of God filling a person completely; the Orthodox tradition, especially, treasures this saying and speaks of people being transformed by God's light. Some listeners here won't share that faith, and the picture still speaks. There's a difference between doing a practice and being lit by it. Between saying the words and meaning them with your whole self. Joseph didn't say pray more. He said: burn.
screen: `WHAT ELSE SHOULD I DO?` · `LOT'S HONEST, HUMBLE LIST.` · `FINGERS LIKE TEN LAMPS.` · `THE LIST IS THE FUEL, NOT THE POINT.` · then, large: `ALL FLAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle and watch it. If you have a candle and a safe place for it, light it now. If not, a lamp will do, or picture one clearly. Settle, and breathe. Look at the flame. Notice it isn't one still thing; it moves, and it's all the way through what it's doing. It doesn't do fire partly. Let your eyes rest there. When your mind starts a list, notice, and come back to the flame. If you pray, you can hold Joseph's words in silence. The bell holds the time.
Become all flame. Abba Joseph's answer to Lot's what else, given with ten fingers lit like lamps. Today's word.
Your line: all flame. Today, pick one ordinary thing you'll do anyway, a conversation, a meal, a task, and do it all the way through, not partly. Day seventy-four.

75.title: The mustard seed
75.hook: Kisa Gotami seeks medicine for her dead child from a house where no one has died (Therigatha commentary)
75.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of Kisa Gotami at funerals and in teaching on impermanence, and she is honored as one of the enlightened nuns whose verses are kept in the Therigatha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba Joseph lifted fingers like ten lamps and said: become all flame. Your line was all flame. What did you do all the way through? Day seventy-five.

Today's story is a tender one, so let's go slowly. Most of us know what happens right after a loss. The world keeps moving, and it feels wrong that it does. People say things that don't help. You may find yourself looking for the one thing, the one call or the one answer, that would undo it. Around two and a half thousand years ago, in northern India, a young mother named Kisa Gotami went looking for exactly that. The Buddhist texts remember her walk. Today's story is the mustard seed.
screen: `AFTER A LOSS.` → `LOOKING FOR THE ONE THING.` → `KISA GOTAMI'S WALK.`

segments.voice: Her name, Kisa Gotami, means something like Gotami the thin one. The story is told in the old Buddhist commentaries, on the poems of the early nuns and on the Dhammapada. She married, and she had a little boy. When he was just old enough to walk, he fell sick and died. And she couldn't accept it. She picked him up and carried him on her hip from house to house in the city, asking everyone for medicine for her son. People turned away, or thought she had lost her mind. Finally someone sent her to the Buddha. And he didn't argue with her. He didn't explain. He said: yes, I can help. Bring me a mustard seed, from a house where no one has ever died. Mustard seed was in every kitchen. It was the easiest thing in the world to ask for. So she went. At the first house, they said: of course, take some. And then: but we lost our father last year. At the next house, a daughter. At the next, a husband, a grandmother, a baby. Every door would give her the seed. No door could give her the seed she needed. Somewhere along that street, the story says, she understood. Death wasn't something that had singled her out. It was in every house. She laid her son down, gently, and came back to the Buddha, and later she became a nun, remembered as one of the wise women of early Buddhism. Look at how the Buddha taught her. Not with a sermon. With a walk, and a houseful of neighbors who knew her grief from the inside. Her sorrow wasn't taken away. She just wasn't alone in it anymore.
screen: `A MOTHER CARRIES HER SON.` · `BRING ONE MUSTARD SEED.` · `EVERY HOUSE HAS LOST SOMEONE.` · `SHE WASN'T ALONE IN IT.` · then, large: `NO HOUSE WITHOUT IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone you've lost, gently. Settle, and breathe. If there's someone, let them come to mind: a face, a voice, a small ordinary moment. You don't have to do anything with it. If tears come, let them. Then, for a moment, think of the other houses on your street, in your town, in the world, where someone is remembering too, right now. Your grief is yours, and it's also in good company. If no one comes to mind, hold someone who's grieving. The bell holds the time.
The mustard seed. The seed every house could give, and no house could give from a home untouched by death. Today's word.
Your line: no house without it. Today, if you pass someone who's grieving, remember that your house knows it too. A small, kind word is enough. Day seventy-five.

76.title: The poisoned arrow
76.hook: the Buddha: a wounded man won't wait to learn who shot him before the arrow comes out (Majjhima Nikaya 63)
76.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the parable of the poisoned arrow to explain why the Buddha set aside certain metaphysical questions and focused on suffering and its ending.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kisa Gotami went door to door for the mustard seed. Your line was no house without it. Were you gentle with someone's grief, or your own? Day seventy-six.

Something goes wrong. The deal falls through, the diagnosis comes back, the text you didn't want arrives. And right away your mind fills with questions. Why did this happen? Whose fault is it? What does it mean about my life? Was it always going to go this way? Those questions can go all night. Some of them matter. But while they're spinning, the actual hurt is still sitting there, untouched. The Buddha had a picture for this, and it's one of the sharpest in all of his teaching. Today's story is the poisoned arrow.
screen: `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.` → `WHY? WHOSE FAULT?` → `THE HURT, STILL UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: It's in the Middle Length Discourses, the Majjhima Nikaya, number sixty-three. A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone and stewing. There are big questions the Buddha has never answered. Is the universe eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or not? Is the soul the same as the body? What happens to an awakened one after death? So he goes to the Buddha and gives him an ultimatum: answer these, or I'm leaving. The Buddha's reply starts with a question of his own: did I ever promise you I'd answer them? And then he tells a story. Imagine a man shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and family rush to bring a surgeon. But the man says: I won't let anyone pull this arrow out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a priest, a merchant, a worker? What was his name, and his family? Was he tall or short, dark or fair? What village did he come from? Was the bow a longbow or a crossbow? What was the string made of? What feathers were on the arrow? And the Buddha says: that man would die before he learned any of it. The questions Malunkyaputta asked aren't foolish, he says; they just don't lead to peace. What he teaches instead is suffering, where it comes from, its ending, and the path to that ending. In other words: the wound, and how to heal it. Buddhists have discussed for centuries what the Buddha's silence on those questions means, and they don't all agree. But the order in the story is clear. First, the arrow comes out. The questions can come after, if they still seem urgent.
screen: `MALUNKYAPUTTA'S ULTIMATUM.` · `A MAN SHOT WITH A POISONED ARROW.` · `WHO SHOT ME? WHAT BOW?` · `FIRST THE WOUND, THEN THE QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `PULL THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pull one arrow instead of asking why. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that's hurting a little today, not the biggest thing, just one. Notice the why questions that come with it: whose fault, what it means, how it happened. Set them to one side for now; they'll keep. Then ask a smaller question: what would help this hurt, right now? A glass of water, an apology, a walk, a phone call, a rest. Find one. Picture doing it. The bell holds the time.
The poisoned arrow. The Buddha's picture of a wounded man who wants every answer before he'll let the surgeon help. Today's word.
Your line: pull the arrow. Today, when something stings, do the one thing that helps before you ask whose fault it was. Day seventy-six.

77.title: The Good Samaritan
77.hook: the man who stopped for the wounded traveler was the one nobody expected (Luke 10:25–37)
77.howItsDone: Christians read the Good Samaritan as Jesus's teaching on loving your neighbor, and churches, hospitals and charities around the world take the name for work that helps strangers in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poisoned arrow, and the man who wanted every answer before the surgeon could help. Your line was pull the arrow. What did you tend to first? Day seventy-seven.

Look back at this week. Rabia with her torch and bucket. Hands on an elephant in the dark. Abba Moses and the sand running out behind him. Fingers like lamps. A mother looking for a mustard seed. An arrow that needed pulling. Sufi, Christian and Buddhist homes, each story kept by its own people. We end the week with a story so famous that its name became an everyday word. Hospitals are named after it. There are laws named after it. And the person it's named for was the one nobody listening expected to be the hero. Today's story is the Good Samaritan.

segments.voice: It's in the Gospel of Luke, chapter ten. An expert in the Jewish law asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus asks what the law says, and the lawyer answers with two commandments joined together: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself. Then the lawyer asks, as the King James puts it, "And who is my neighbour?" Jesus answers with a story. A man is going down the steep road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robbers strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead. A priest comes along, sees him, and "passed by on the other side." A Levite, a temple assistant, does the same. The text never says why. Then a Samaritan comes. Samaritans and Jews in that time had centuries of bad blood between them; each side had reasons to distrust the other. And this Samaritan stops. He bandages the wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, pays the innkeeper two coins, and says: whatever more it costs, I'll repay you when I come back. Then Jesus turns the lawyer's question around. Not who counts as my neighbor, but which of these three acted like a neighbor? And the lawyer answers: the one who showed him mercy. Jesus says, "Go, and do thou likewise." Remember, this is a Jewish teacher telling a Jewish lawyer a story built on the Jewish commandment to love your neighbor. The story isn't a case against priests or Levites. Its surprise is that the helper came from the people the listeners least expected, and that being a neighbor turned out to be something you do, not something you're owed.
screen: `WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR?` · `PRIEST AND LEVITE PASS BY.` · `THE SAMARITAN STOPS AND PAYS.` · `WHO ACTED LIKE A NEIGHBOR?` · then, large: `GO AND DO LIKEWISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for one person today. Settle, and breathe. Think about the roads you'll travel today, real or online: the hallway, the bus, the checkout line, the family group chat. Picture one place where someone might need a little help, and where it would be easy to pass by on the other side. Now picture stopping. Not a grand rescue; a door held, a question asked, a few minutes given. Notice what makes stopping hard, busyness, awkwardness, and let it be there. The bell holds the time.
The Good Samaritan. The traveler nobody expected, who stopped, bandaged, carried and paid, and turned the question of who's my neighbor into what does a neighbor do. Today's word.
Your line: go and do likewise. Today, stop for one person you'd usually pass, and give them a few minutes of real help. Day seventy-seven.
